description: Davis and Moore on why some roles must be more rewarded than others, and the feminist and Marxist case against.
content_html:
What Is Social Stratification?

Social stratification refers to the system by which society ranks categories of people in a hierarchy. In every known human society, some groups enjoy greater wealth, status and power than others. Sociologists explain this unequal ordering in very different ways, depending on their perspective. This lesson examines the functionalist explanation of why stratification exists, before considering how rival perspectives challenge it.

Key Fact

Davis and Moore (1945) argued that social stratification is a “universal necessity” — every society that has ever existed has developed some form of ranked hierarchy. They believed this was not a flaw in social organisation but a functional requirement for society’s survival.

Davis and Moore: Functionalist Theory of Stratification

Writing from a functionalist perspective, Kingsley Davis and Wilbert Moore (1945) argued that social stratification performs two essential tasks for society: effective role allocation and performance linked to rewards. Their argument runs as follows.

First, societies contain positions that vary in their functional importance — some roles are more critical to the smooth running of society than others. A surgeon operating on a patient in an NHS hospital, for example, performs a role that requires a high level of skill and years of specialist training. Second, the pool of talented individuals capable of performing such roles is, in their view, limited. Society must therefore motivate the most talented people to fill these functionally important roles by attaching high rewards — high pay, prestige and status — to them.

The promise of greater rewards encourages individuals to undergo the long training required, work hard and perform these roles conscientiously. The result is a meritocracy — a society in which positions are filled on the basis of ability and effort, not birth. Davis and Moore concluded that stratification is therefore not only inevitable but socially necessary. Unequal rewards, in this view, are the mechanism by which societies ensure the right people end up doing the most important jobs.

Stratification systems differ in how rigid they are. An open system is one in which social mobility is possible — individuals can move up or down the hierarchy through their own efforts. Contemporary capitalist societies such as the UK are described as relatively open systems, where educational qualifications and occupational achievement can enable movement across class boundaries. Davis and Moore’s model assumes an open, meritocratic system.

A closed system is one in which social position is fixed at birth and movement between positions is not permitted. The most extreme example is the caste system, historically practised in parts of South Asia, in which occupation, marriage and social interaction were all determined by the caste a person was born into. Slavery is another closed system. Critics note that the UK class system has elements of both: educational qualifications and hard work can improve life chances, but evidence consistently shows that social class background remains a strong predictor of outcomes.

Criticisms of Davis and Moore

Davis and Moore’s theory has attracted sustained criticism from several perspectives. A key early critic was Melvin Tumin, who challenged the assumption that talent is scarce and that high rewards are the only way to motivate people. Tumin questioned whether it is possible to measure “functional importance” objectively. He noted that some highly rewarded occupations (such as entertainment celebrities) have questionable functional value, while roles that are arguably essential to society (such as refuse collection or care work) are poorly rewarded.

Tumin also argued that stratification actually restricts the talent pool by creating barriers: individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds face material obstacles to accessing higher education and professional training regardless of their ability. This means stratification may reduce, not increase, the chances of the most talented filling the most important roles.

A common misconception is to accept Davis and Moore’s theory as simply “common sense” and assume that high earners must be in their positions because of talent. The sociological critique challenges this. Ascribed status — status passed down through family wealth, social networks or inherited privilege — continues to play a significant role in determining who fills elite positions. Research consistently shows that privately educated individuals are over-represented in top professions in the UK. This suggests stratification may reflect inherited advantage as much as merit, a point that Marxist and feminist perspectives develop further.

Marxist and Feminist Critiques

From a Marxist perspective, stratification is not a neutral mechanism for allocating talent — it is a system that serves the interests of the bourgeoisie by legitimising exploitation. Marx argued that the ruling class uses ideology to make inequality appear natural and inevitable, concealing the fact that the system primarily benefits those who already own wealth and property. From this view, Davis and Moore’s theory functions as ruling class ideology — it justifies the existing unequal distribution of rewards as though it were based purely on merit.

Feminist sociologists point out that Davis and Moore’s model fails to account for patriarchy. Women have historically been excluded from or under-rewarded in many functionally important roles not because of lack of talent, but because of structural discrimination. Even if the principle of attaching high rewards to important roles were valid, the definition of which roles are “important” has historically been made by men. Care work, nursing and teaching — predominantly female occupations — tend to be rewarded less highly than male-dominated professions requiring comparable training, suggesting that reward levels reflect gender power relations rather than functional necessity alone.

Key Fact

In a 12-mark Discuss question on stratification, you should present at least three perspectives: functionalist (Davis and Moore — meritocratic necessity), Marxist (stratification serves ruling-class interests, perpetuates exploitation), and feminist (stratification reflects patriarchy, not just merit or functional importance).
exam_tip_html: On a 12-mark Discuss question about stratification, the most common error is giving only a functionalist account of Davis and Moore without any counter-perspectives. The mark scheme rewards candidates who present arguments for the statement (citing Davis and Moore’s meritocratic argument) and arguments against (citing Marxist exploitation theory or feminist critiques of patriarchal reward structures). A Mastering-tier answer will name at least two contrasting perspectives with sociological vocabulary (meritocracy, bourgeoisie, patriarchy, ascribed status) and close with a supported judgement about which perspective offers the most convincing explanation — not simply listing both sides.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Davis and Moore (1945) argued that stratification is a universal necessity: unequal rewards attached to functionally important roles ensure effective role allocation and motivated performance in a meritocratic system.
  • Critics including Tumin challenged whether functional importance can be objectively measured and whether talent is as scarce as Davis and Moore assumed; he argued stratification can restrict the talent pool by creating barriers for those from lower socioeconomic backgrounds.
  • Marxist and feminist perspectives reject the meritocratic claim: Marxists argue stratification serves ruling-class interests and perpetuates exploitation; feminists argue it reflects patriarchal power relations rather than neutral functional necessity.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the functionalist view of social stratification?
A) Stratification is a system that benefits only the wealthy
B) Stratification is a universal necessity that ensures the most talented fill the most important roles
C) Stratification is a form of patriarchal control over women
D) Stratification is a social construct with no functional purpose
practice_questions.marks: B) Stratification is a universal necessity that ensures the most talented fill the most important roles [1 mark]

1 mark for identifying that meritocracy is a system based on individual ability/achievement; 1 mark for explaining that social position is determined by talent and effort rather than inherited privilege or birth. Example of a full answer: 'A meritocracy is a system in which people's social positions are determined by their own talent and effort rather than by their family background or inherited wealth.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one criticism of Davis and Moore's functionalist theory of stratification.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a criticism (e.g. Tumin questioned whether functional importance can be objectively measured; feminist critique that gender bias distorts reward structures; Marxist argument that stratification serves ruling-class interests rather than society as a whole). 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'Tumin argued that it is impossible to measure which roles are genuinely most important to society, noting that care workers and refuse collectors perform essential work yet are poorly rewarded compared with entertainers or senior executives whose functional importance to society is less obvious.'

practice_questions.text: Describe how a Marxist sociologist would explain social stratification.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Students should include: Marx argued that stratification arises from the relationship between social groups and the means of production (1 mark); the bourgeoisie own the means of production and exploit the labour of the proletariat (1 mark); ruling class ideology makes this inequality appear natural and legitimate (1 mark); from a Marxist view, Davis and Moore's theory functions as ideology that justifies an exploitative system rather than a neutral meritocratic one (1 mark). Any two developed points linked to named Marxist concepts earn full marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe one way a feminist sociologist might challenge the Davis and Moore thesis about stratification.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Students should describe: feminists argue that the definition of 'functionally important roles' has historically been shaped by patriarchal values, not objective criteria (1 mark); predominantly female occupations such as nursing and care work require significant training and are essential to society but are rewarded less than male-dominated professions of comparable importance (1 mark); this suggests reward levels reflect gender power relations rather than functional necessity (1 mark); Walby's concept of patriarchy as a structure that operates across paid employment helps explain why women's labour continues to be under-rewarded even in formally equal systems (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Sociologists agree that inequality in modern society is the result of a fair and meritocratic system. How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A full range of relevant arguments is presented from at least two contrasting perspectives. Davis and Moore's functionalist thesis is explained in detail — unequal rewards attached to functionally important roles, meritocratic role allocation, motivating talented individuals. At least one contrasting perspective is developed in equal depth: Marxist (stratification serves bourgeoisie, ruling class ideology, exploitation of proletariat) and/or feminist (patriarchal reward structures, gender pay gap, historically male-defined 'functional importance'). Named sociologists or concepts are used throughout. A clear, supported judgement weighs the evidence and reaches a substantiated conclusion about whether meritocracy is a convincing explanation of inequality.

Secure: Most relevant arguments present, both sides covered, named sociologists referenced. Clear judgement at the end though development may be uneven.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided, or two-sided but undeveloped. Some named theorists referenced. Conclusion present but assertive rather than substantiated.

Emerging: Basic points, mostly description rather than evaluation. Few or no named sociologists. Little or no judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: According to Davis and Moore, what is the main purpose of attaching high rewards to important roles?
options: To reward people for inherited talent
To motivate the most talented individuals to fill functionally important positions
To create a rigid class system that preserves order
To ensure the bourgeoisie retain control of society

knowledge_checks.q: Which sociologist first described social stratification as a 'universal necessity' from a functionalist perspective?
A stratification system in which social position is fixed at birth and movement between groups is not permitted is called a _____ system.
Davis and Moore argued that only a _____ pool of talented people exists who can fill the most important roles in society.
Match each perspective to its view of social stratification:
right: Stratification is a meritocratic necessity that allocates talent to important roles
Stratification serves ruling-class interests and legitimises exploitation
Stratification reflects patriarchal power relations, not neutral functional importance

flashcard_questions.q: What did Davis and Moore (1945) argue about social stratification?
flashcard_questions.a: That it is a universal necessity ensuring talented people fill functionally important roles through unequal rewards.

flashcard_questions.q: What term describes a system where social position is determined by talent and effort rather than birth?
What are 'functionally important roles' in Davis and Moore's theory?
flashcard_questions.a: Roles essential to society's survival requiring high skill or responsibility, justified in being highly rewarded.
The ranking of society into a hierarchy of layers, with the most privileged at the top.
Social position determined by birth or family background rather than personal achievement.
Social position earned through individual effort, qualifications or merit.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a closed stratification system?
flashcard_questions.a: A hierarchy in which social position is fixed at birth and movement between groups is not permitted.

flashcard_questions.q: What is an open stratification system?
flashcard_questions.a: A hierarchy in which social mobility is possible through individual effort or achievement.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Tumin argue against Davis and Moore?
flashcard_questions.a: That functional importance cannot be objectively measured and stratification restricts the talent pool.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Marxist view of Davis and Moore's theory?
flashcard_questions.a: That it functions as ruling-class ideology, making exploitation appear natural and meritocratic.
A system in which men hold structural power and women are systematically disadvantaged.

flashcard_questions.q: How do feminists criticise Davis and Moore's theory of stratification?
flashcard_questions.a: Reward structures reflect patriarchal values, not objective functional importance, disadvantaging female-dominated roles.

glossary_terms.definition: The way society is divided into a hierarchy of layers, with the most privileged at the top and the least privileged at the bottom.
A system in which social position is determined by individual talent, effort and achievement rather than inherited privilege.
Positions in society that are essential to its survival and smooth running, requiring high levels of skill or responsibility.
Social position determined at birth or through family background rather than by personal achievement.
Social position earned through individual effort, qualifications or merit.
In Marxist theory, a set of ideas promoted by the ruling class to make the existing unequal social order appear natural and legitimate.
A system in which men hold structural power and women are systematically disadvantaged across social institutions.
A sociological perspective that sees society as a system of interrelated parts, each performing a necessary function for the whole.

hero_image_caption: Social stratification describes the hierarchy of rewards and privileges found in every known society.
